title: Rutledge v. Clearway Energy Group LLC
description: Whether Senate Bill 21's amendments to the Delaware General Corporation Law, specifically its safe harbor provisions and retroactive application, violate the Delaware Constitution by divesting the Court of Chancery of equitable jurisdiction or eliminating accrued causes of action.
plaintiff_argument: Thomas Drew Rutledge argued that SB 21's safe harbor provisions unconstitutionally divest the Court of Chancery of its equitable jurisdiction and that its retroactive application eliminates vested causes of action, violating the Delaware Constitution.
defendant_argument: Clearway Defendants and the Governor argued that SB 21 does not reduce the Court of Chancery's jurisdiction but rather provides a statutory review framework, and that the General Assembly has the constitutional authority to legislate on matters of equity, including retroactive application.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that Senate Bill 21's amendments are constitutional, finding that they neither divest the Court of Chancery of its equitable jurisdiction nor impermissibly extinguish any vested rights.

title: In re Covid-related Restrictions on Religious Services
description: Whether the Governor's COVID-19 restrictions on religious services violated constitutional rights and whether the Governor is immune from suit for these actions.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the Governor's COVID-19 restrictions on religious services violated their constitutional rights, including free exercise, free speech, free assembly, and equal protection, and that the Governor was not immune from suit.
defendant_argument: The Governor argued that the restrictions were a necessary exercise of discretionary emergency powers to protect public health, and that he was immune from suit under state tort claims act and qualified immunity doctrines.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court affirmed the lower courts' dismissals, holding that the claims for injunctive relief were not justiciable due to the restrictions being lifted, and the claims for damages were barred by the Governor's immunity.

title: Albence v. Mennella
description: Whether the plaintiffs, a citizen and a state senator, have standing to challenge Delaware's permanent absentee voting and early voting statutes as unconstitutional.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the permanent absentee and early voting statutes violate the Delaware Constitution and dilute their votes, and that they have standing as an election inspector, a candidate, and registered voters.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the plaintiffs lacked standing to challenge the statutes because they failed to establish imminent or particularized harm, and that the statutes are constitutional.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the Superior Court's judgment, vacated its declaratory judgment, and dismissed the amended complaint for lack of standing, allowing the challenged statutes to remain in effect for 2024 elections.

title: Burroughs v. State
description: Whether the Delaware bail system, which allows for unaffordable financial conditions for pretrial release, violates the Equal Protection Clause, substantive and procedural due process, or Article I, § 12 of the Delaware Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: Burroughs argued that the Delaware bail system, by imposing unaffordable cash bail leading to pretrial detention, violates his fundamental rights to equal protection and due process, and the state constitutional right to bail, especially when less restrictive alternatives could address public safety concerns.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the bail system is constitutional, as it is rationally related to the legitimate and compelling governmental interest in ensuring public safety and the defendant's appearance in court, and that the procedural protections in place are sufficient.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Superior Court's judgment, holding that the Delaware bail system, including the use of unaffordable cash bail for pretrial detention, does not violate the Equal Protection Clause, the Due Process Clause (provided procedural protections are observed), or Article I, § 12 of the Delaware Constitution.

title: State v. Higgin
description: Whether the recently enacted Same-Day Registration Statute and Vote-by-Mail Statute are constitutional under Article V of the Delaware Constitution, with the plaintiff arguing they conflict with constitutional provisions and the defendant arguing they are valid exercises of legislative power.
plaintiff_argument: The Same-Day Registration Statute conflicts with Article V, Section 4's voter registration deadlines and appeal processes, and the Vote-by-Mail Statute violates Article V, Section 4A by expanding absentee voting beyond constitutionally specified categories.
defendant_argument: The statutes are valid exercises of legislative power, arguing that mail-in voting is distinct from absentee voting, or that Section 4A sets a minimum for absentee voting categories, not an exhaustive list, and that Section 4's registration window establishes a constitutional floor, not a ceiling.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Court of Chancery's invalidation of the Vote-by-Mail Statute and reversed its upholding of the Same-Day Registration Statute, concluding both statutes violate the Delaware Constitution.

title: In re Opinion of the Justices
description: Whether Article III, Section 13 of the Delaware Constitution, concerning the removal of public officials by the Governor upon address of the General Assembly, allows for lesser actions like suspension, considers an indictment alone as reasonable cause, and requires specific hearing procedures and notice.
plaintiff_argument: The General Assembly sought clarification, potentially hoping for broader interpretations of their powers, such as allowing suspension as a lesser action, considering an indictment as sufficient reasonable cause, and flexibility in hearing procedures.
defendant_argument: The court clarified that the Governor's authority under Section 13 does not include suspension, an indictment alone is not sufficient for "reasonable cause," and specific hearing and notice requirements (including due process elements) are mandatory.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court provided an advisory opinion to the General Assembly, clarifying that under Article III, Section 13, "reasonable cause" for removal may include an indictment but an indictment alone is insufficient, the authority to remove does not include suspension, a hearing is required prior to a vote on a bill of address (which can be in the first House or joint), and specific due process elements must be afforded during the hearing. There is no appeal from the Governor's decision.
